title: The day the wind stopped
hookLine: when baby Hanuman fell, his father the wind stopped moving, and every creature learned what breath is
carry: prana: slow breath thins the veil

lines: THE WIND CARRIES HIM INTO A CAVE.
cards: You met this baby in year one. Hanuman, son of the wind, wakes up hungry, sees the rising sun, takes it for a ripe fruit, and leaps for it. Indra, king of the gods, strikes him with the thunderbolt, and the child falls.
Today, the part that comes next, told from the wind's side. In the Ramayana's last book, Vayu, the wind, gathers up his hurt son and carries him into a cave. And he stops.
Not only the breeze in the trees. The wind inside every living thing stops moving.

teach.h: VAYU STOPS, AND NO ONE CAN BREATHE.
teach.b: No one can breathe. Gods, people, animals, all of them begin to choke. They run to Brahma, the creator, and Brahma goes to the cave himself and touches the child, and Hanuman wakes.
Only then does the wind move again, and the gods heap gifts on the boy. Here's what Hindus take from it: breath isn't just air.
It's prana, life itself, and the old texts treat it as holy. A prayer chanted at the start of the Taittiriya Upanishad greets the wind: salutations to you, Vayu; you are Brahman made visible.

That's why breath work sits inside Hindu worship, not beside it. Many Hindus who keep the morning sandhya do pranayama, measured breathing, just before the Gayatri mantra. Patanjali makes it the fourth limb of yoga.
Sutra 2.49: once the seat is steady, pranayama is pausing the flow of in-breath and out-breath.
Sutra 2.50: the breath becomes long and subtle. Not forceful. Long and fine, like thread.

teach.h: THE COVERING OVER THE LIGHT THINS.
teach.b: Then the reason, in 2.52: from this, the covering over the light thins. The light is the mind's own clarity. It was never missing, only covered.
And 2.53: the mind becomes fit for concentration. A practical note: strong breath-holding is learned in person, with a teacher, and none of it is needed here.
So before a prayer, or an exam, or a hard talk, you don't have to add anything.

teach.h: PRANA: SLOW BREATH THINS THE VEIL.
teach.b: Let the breath that keeps every creature alive grow slow, and the light that was already there shows through.

how: Many Hindus practice pranayama as part of daily worship, for instance before reciting the Gayatri mantra in the morning, and yoga teachers usually introduce breath retention gradually and under supervision.

o: holding the breath for as long as you can bear it
counting your breaths aloud to fall asleep
working with the breath, letting it grow long and fine

games.q: the wind and the breath — tap the pairs.

s: when Vayu stopped, only the breeze in the trees went still
in the epic, the wind inside every creature stopped, and no one could breathe.
many Hindus do pranayama just before the Gayatri mantra
it's part of the morning sandhya in many homes.
the sutras call for forceful, heroic breathing
2.50 says the breath becomes long and subtle.

games.q: before the gayatri, many hindus sit and breathe slowly for a minute. by sutra 2.52, what is that breathing doing?
o: thinning the covering over the mind's light, so the prayer can land.
games.why: 2.52: from pranayama, the covering over the light thins. 2.53: the mind grows fit to focus. so the breath comes first, then the prayer.

practice: Sit steady and easy, and let each out-breath be a little longer than the in-breath, with no strain and no holding. Make the breath so quiet you could barely hear it, and if you ever feel short of air, go back to normal breathing.
If you pray, let this be the minute before your prayer, as many Hindus do before the Gayatri. Then notice whether anything clears.

wordCard.voice: Pranayama. Working with the life breath, letting it grow long and subtle, the fourth limb of yoga.

orig.note: Sanskrit prāṇāyāma: prāṇa (life breath) plus āyāma (extension), or yama (restraint); the fourth limb.

carryVoice: Your line: prana: slow breath thins the veil. The light was never gone; it was only covered. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda 35–36 (Vayu withdraws with the infant Hanuman; creatures cannot breathe; Brahma revives him; the gods' gifts)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.1.1 (salutation to Vayu, Brahman made visible)
Yoga Sutra 2.49–2.50 (pausing the flow of breath; the breath grows long and subtle)
Yoga Sutra 2.52–2.53 (the covering of the light dwindles; fitness for concentration)
